DOCUMENT:
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone" -- 99 students x £9,250 = £915,750, about £0.9 million, not £1.2 million.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation." -- Students opted in, and the document reports mentees were more likely to live in halls (78% vs 52%) and to have higher entry qualifications, both associated with continuation. Self-selection and these confounders mean the gap does not show that mentoring caused higher continuation.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in" -- Scaling to 4,100 students at eight mentees per mentor needs about 513 mentors, but the document reports the University could fill only 155 of 200 advertised posts. The recommendation and costing assume mentor supply scales and never address the stated recruitment constraint (nor that automatically enrolled students may benefit less than volunteers).

REVIEW:
# Review: Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26

## Summary

The outcome data are strong: they are complete, come from enrolment records, and cover the whole cohort. The main problem is how they are interpreted. The report treats the 8-point gap between self-selected mentees and everyone else as the causal effect of mentoring, and it never tests that assumption. The report's own data suggest the true effect is much smaller. Several downstream figures also have arithmetic or feasibility problems:

- the £1.2m benefit is miscalculated;
- the roll-out projection to 94% assumes the full gap is causal;
- the roll-out costing ignores the recruitment constraint.

The recommendation may still be right, but the report does not yet support it with the confidence claimed.

## Major issues

### 1. The 8-point gap is not evidence that mentoring works (selection bias)

Participation was opt-in, first-come-first-served in welcome week. Section 3 shows mentees differed from non-mentees in ways known to predict continuation:
- **78% vs 52% living in halls.** Living in halls is one of the strongest predictors of first-year continuation.
- **Higher entry tariff.** Tariff is also a strong predictor of continuation.
- **Early, motivated opt-in.** Places went within two weeks, so these students were already engaged.

Any or all of these could produce a large gap even if mentoring had no effect. Comparing mentees on age and gender does nothing to address these differences. The conclusion that the gap is "clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation" (Section 4) and "has shown" an 8-point improvement (Section 7) does not follow from the data.

### 2. The report's own figures point to a much smaller effect

- If mentoring caused 99 extra continuers, mentees would have continued at 86% without it. Overall continuation would then have been about 86%, a drop from 87% the previous year.
- In fact overall continuation rose only 1.4 points (87% to 88.4%). If 99 extra continuers were added to an otherwise stable cohort, the rise would be about 2.4 points.
- Non-mentees (86%) did worse than the previous year's whole cohort (87%). That is what you would expect if stronger students moved into the mentored group, not if mentoring added students.

At face value, the year-on-year change is consistent with an effect nearer 1–1.5 points across the cohort, roughly 50–60 students. Even that figure is not attributable to mentoring without controlling for cohort differences between years.

### 3. A better comparison group was available and not used

The **300-student waiting list** wanted mentoring but did not get it. Their continuation rate is the obvious comparison, since they share the motivation to opt in. At a minimum, the report should:
- give the waiting-list continuation rate;
- compare mentees and non-mentees within the same groups (in halls vs not, by tariff band, by faculty), or use a regression or matched comparison controlling for these factors.

Without this, the effect size is unknown.

### 4. The £1.2 million figure is miscalculated

99 students × £9,250 = **£915,750**, not £1.2m. Even with the effect taken at face value, the benefit is overstated by about 30%. In addition:
- Fee income is gross, not net. Retained students carry teaching and support costs.
- If the true effect is nearer 50–60 students (see issue 2), the benefit is roughly £0.5m.

### 5. The roll-out projection assumes everything the pilot did not show

Section 6 says automatic allocation would lift the whole cohort to about 94%. This assumes:
- the full 8-point gap is causal (see issues 1–3);
- students who **did not** opt in would benefit as much as those who did. Students allocated automatically are likely to engage less, and the students most at risk may be the least likely to take part;
- the effect holds for students outside halls and with lower tariffs, groups that were under-represented in the pilot.

No data on engagement are reported (attendance at group sessions, use of one-to-one meetings). So we cannot tell whether benefits are linked to actually taking part.

### 6. The roll-out costing ignores the binding constraint: mentor supply

The author says costing is "built directly from actual pilot spending per mentee". The arithmetic (4,100 × £174 ≈ £714k) is correct, but the pilot shows the constraint is recruitment, not money:
- **4,100 mentees ÷ 8 = about 513 mentors**, 3.3 times the 155 recruited.
- The pilot filled only 155 of 200 advertised posts.

Recruiting more than three times as many mentors will probably require higher pay, more recruitment effort, or larger groups. Each of these raises cost or may dilute the effect. Coordination (one coordinator per faculty) also may not scale in line with mentee numbers. The report needs a recruitment plan and a costing that reflects it.

## Minor issues

- **Survey rating (4.3/5):** no response rate is given. Respondents at the end of the year are by definition mostly students who stayed. Satisfaction is not evidence of an effect on continuation and should not be described as reinforcing "the numbers".
- **"Large by any standard":** the size of the raw gap is not in question. Its attribution is.
- **"Pays for itself many times over" (Section 7):** even on the uncorrected figures this is about 4×. On a corrected, bias-adjusted estimate the margin is much thinner, though it may still be positive.
- **Single year, single institution:** this is worth noting as a limitation, along with any changes in other support services in 2025-26.
- **Mentor benefits** (confidence, employability) are self-reported and are not part of the continuation case.

## Recommendations

1. Report the waiting-list group's continuation rate as the main comparison.
2. Run an adjusted analysis that controls for accommodation, tariff, faculty and other available predictors such as widening-participation markers and commuter status.
3. Correct the fee income figure and present it as a range based on the adjusted effect, net of marginal costs.
4. Report engagement data and analyse the outcome by level of engagement.
5. Re-cost the roll-out around realistic mentor recruitment of about 513 posts.
6. Consider a **staged or randomised expansion** for 2026-27, for example allocating mentors by lottery or rolling out faculty by faculty. This would give a robust estimate of the effect before committing about £714k a year.
7. Change the tone of Sections 4 and 7 from "clear evidence" and "has shown" to "promising but not yet established".

## Bottom line

The scheme may well help, and mentees value it. However, the headline 8-point effect, the £1.2m benefit and the 94% roll-out projection all rest on comparing a self-selected, advantaged group with everyone else. The report's own year-on-year figures suggest the real effect is substantially smaller. The case for extension needs a proper comparison group and a realistic mentor-recruitment plan before it can be described as well-evidenced.
